lines.say: When should a patient restart an already-prescribed pollen spray? And if our own alert rule fails to beat the forecast, would we say so?

Open the live demo with zero keys. On Valencia's May twenty-eighth replay, pollen stays below threshold, so zero reminders fire. Switch to Madrid's May eighteenth grass spike: deterministic code drafts one hundred eleven reminders, and a nurse approves every batch.

Weather APIs model an eleven-kilometre grid; people breathe near point traps. We checked five years of Open-Meteo forecasts against Madrid, Basel, and Zürich traps — seven thousand three hundred seventy-three city-days.
Six rules were frozen in the repo before scoring: testing day rules P2 against R1, and pre-peak onset R2 against P2 and climatology across twenty-eight seasons — including missed seasons.
Across eight hundred sixty-three high-pollen events, the API forecast caught forty-one point six percent. Our rule caught forty-one point zero. It did not beat the API.
So the app uses the API forecast, and our work went into what happens next.

Code filters who gets a draft, and a nurse approves every batch. Thirty-four patients without a medicine on file are blocked automatically. Each draft names only the medicine class already on file. Not a medical device.
Honest limits: even the API forecast catches only thirteen point six percent of Madrid olive spikes. Pre-peak lead reflects look-ahead, not beating climatology. Valencia is never scored.
Zero unapproved sends, eighty-nine of two hundred filtered out by code, and ninety-five green tests. Open the live PollenPlan demo today — zero setup required.
